nameStory: The Mediterranean katydid gets its name from its origins around the Mediterranean Sea, where it's native to southern Europe and North Africa. It's also called the southern sickle bush-cricket because of the curved, sickle-shaped egg-laying tube (ovipositor) that females use to insert eggs into plant stems. The 'katydid' part comes from the rhythmic calls that sound like 'Katy-did, Katy-didn't' in some species, though this particular species has its own unique song.
description: The Mediterranean katydid is a slender, green grasshopper-like insect that's actually more closely related to crickets than true grasshoppers. These delicate-looking insects have long, thread-like antennae that are often longer than their bodies and prominent hind legs built for jumping. They're relatively small katydids, typically measuring about an inch long, with narrow wings that extend beyond their body. Originally from Europe, they've become established in parts of New England as an introduced species.

idTips.label: Body shape and color
idTips.description: Bright green, slender body with a delicate, almost translucent appearance - much thinner than most grasshoppers you'll encounter

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Extremely long, hair-thin antennae that are typically longer than the entire body and constantly moving as the insect explores

idTips.label: Wings
idTips.description: Narrow, clear wings that extend well beyond the tip of the abdomen, with visible green veining that catches the light

idTips.label: Female ovipositor
idTips.description: Females have a distinctive curved, blade-like egg-laying tube at the rear that resembles a small sickle - firm to the touch if you can observe one up close

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Long, spiny hind legs with tiny barbs you can feel if you gently handle one - built for powerful jumping

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Notably smaller and more delicate than most native katydids, with a fragile appearance that makes them seem almost fairy-like

habitat: Mediterranean katydids prefer gardens, parks, and edge habitats with mixed vegetation including shrubs, ornamental plants, and weedy areas. They're often found on roses, fruit trees, and other cultivated plants in suburban and urban settings. Look for them in areas with a mix of native and non-native plants, particularly where there's some shelter from wind and plenty of foliage to hide among during the day.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in late spring, often found resting on new foliage during warm afternoons. This is when you're most likely to spot their bright green coloration against fresh leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults most visible and vocal. Listen for their distinctive calls at dusk and look for them feeding on plant material and small insects on shrubs and garden plants.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active into early fall, with females busy laying eggs in plant stems using their sickle-shaped ovipositors. Calling may decrease but individuals are still findable on vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with frost, and the species overwinters as eggs inserted into plant stems. No adults visible during the cold months.

funFact: Mediterranean katydids are musical immigrants - they've brought their own European 'accent' to New England soundscapes, with calls that are distinctly different from native katydids, creating entirely new nighttime symphonies in areas where they've established.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with young or small native katydids, but Mediterranean katydids are consistently more slender and delicate-looking with proportionally longer antennae. Remember: if it looks almost too fragile to be real and has antennae like green hair, it's probably Mediterranean.
contextualKnowledge: As an introduced species, Mediterranean katydids represent how global trade and climate change are reshaping New England's insect communities. While they don't appear to be major agricultural pests here, their establishment shows how easily small insects can hitchhike to new continents and adapt to different climates.
compareHints: Since this is the only Phaneroptera species established in New England, compare it to native katydids in the broader bush-cricket family. Mediterranean katydids are much more delicate and slender than robust native species like the greater angle-wing katydid, with thinner wings, longer antennae relative to body size, and a more translucent appearance. They lack the broad, leaf-like wing covers of many native katydids.
